analysis.one_liner: Extends workplace break-time and private-space protections for nursing mothers to all workers, not just hourly ones.
analysis.headline: After its January 2020 introduction, the bill was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and never moved again; it died when the 116th Congress ended without a vote in either chamber.
analysis.plain_summary: A 2010 law already required employers to give hourly, non-exempt workers reasonable breaks and a private, non-bathroom space to pump breast milk. This bill would close the gap by extending those same protections to salaried and other workers the 2010 law left out, and it would require employers to pay hourly workers for pumping time when they are not fully relieved of duty during the break. It would also let workers sue to enforce the right, the same way they enforce other wage-law rights.
analysis.who_benefits: Nursing mothers working in jobs not covered by the 2010 rule — most salaried employees, teachers, nurses, farmworkers, and other workers who were excluded from the overtime and break provisions of the Fair Labor Standards Act. Under this bill they would get the same right to reasonable pumping breaks and a private space, and hourly workers who keep working through a break would be paid for that time.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Fair Labor Standards Act so that the pumping-break and private-space protections apply to salaried and other categories of workers excluded under existing law.
It requires employers to pay hourly workers for pumping break time when they are not entirely relieved from duty during the break.
It gives nursing workers a private right of action, letting them sue employers who deny the accommodation, by adding the pumping provision to the enforcement section of the wage law.
The expanded coverage would take effect 120 days after enactment, with the pay and enforcement provisions effective immediately.

analysis.who_pays: Covered employers — retail chains, hospitals, schools, offices, and other businesses — would bear the cost of providing reasonable breaks and a private pumping space for all employees, including salaried staff they had never had to accommodate, and of paying hourly workers for pumping time spent not fully off duty. The burdens are modest and bounded: the law already requires breaks to be reasonable, and small firms with under 50 employees could claim an undue-hardship exemption under the underlying statute.

drawbacks.text: Extending break and space requirements to salaried and previously exempt workers adds compliance costs for employers, including workplaces where a private space is difficult to arrange, such as schools, hospitals, and small worksites.
Paying hourly workers for pumping breaks when they are not entirely relieved from duty creates a new pay obligation that employers would have to track and administer.

Critics of the existing accommodation mandate have argued that break and space requirements impose scheduling burdens on small businesses and can complicate staffing, and this bill widens the set of businesses covered by that mandate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits run to millions of working mothers, including the many salaried workers the 2010 law left out, and the costs to employers are real but modest — reasonable breaks, a private space, and pay only when a worker keeps working through a break. The main design trade-off is the compliance burden on workplaces where private space is hard to find, but the bill keeps the existing 'reasonable' standard and the existing small-business undue-hardship exemption rather than imposing a rigid mandate.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Carolyn Maloney introduced the bill on January 13, 2020, with six cosponsors — five Democrats and one Republican.
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Education and Labor.
No committee action, hearing, markup, or floor vote followed; the complete action history shows no activity after the referral.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill died without a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers whose salaried and other workers were outside the 2010 pumping-accommodation rule never faced the new coverage, pay, or enforcement obligations. Working mothers in those jobs gained nothing during this Congress; the committee that held the bill and the House that never considered it preserved the status quo.

for.name: Rep. Carolyn B. Maloney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the PUMP for Nursing Mothers Act to extend federal pumping-break protections to workers not covered by the 2010 law.

for.name: 1 of 197 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it bipartisan at introduction.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Rep. Bobby Scott, D-VA)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 13, 2020 and never acted on the bill; no markup, hearing, or report was scheduled before the Congress ended.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; it remained in committee for the rest of the 116th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan but thin: all six cosponsors included one Republican among five Democrats, and no votes were ever taken.

industries.industry: Employers with salaried and previously exempt workers
industries.note: The bill would extend break-time, private-space, and (for hourly staff working through breaks) paid-break obligations to salaried and other workers the 2010 rule did not cover, adding compliance and pay costs. The industry's preference to avoid those obligations runs against the workers seeking the accommodation.

By adding the pumping provision to the Fair Labor Standards Act's private-enforcement section, the bill creates a right workers could sue to enforce. That gain exists only if the underlying accommodation right is meaningful, so it lines up with workers' interests.
